source: The weather was terrible, but we had a great time.
correct: Although the weather was terrible, we had a great time.
explanation: <Although> + clause introduces a concession (unexpected contrast).

source: Although he worked overtime, he didn't finish the project.
correct: Despite working overtime, he didn't finish the project.
explanation: <Despite> + gerund/noun replaces <Although> + full clause.

prompt: Rewrite using <In spite of the fact that>
source: Despite being exhausted, she continued running.
correct: In spite of the fact that she was exhausted, she continued running.
explanation: <In spite of the fact that> + clause is a more formal version of <despite>.

source: The hotel was expensive. The service was poor.
correct: The hotel was expensive. However, the service was poor.
The hotel was expensive; however, the service was poor.
explanation: <However> links contrasting sentences. It's followed by a comma.

source: The critics hated the film, but it was a commercial success.
correct: The critics hated the film. Nevertheless, it was a commercial success.
The critics hated the film; nevertheless, it was a commercial success.
explanation: <Nevertheless> = <Despite that>, more formal than <however>.

source: The lecture was very boring. Half the audience fell asleep.
correct: The lecture was so boring that half the audience fell asleep.
explanation: <So> + adjective/adverb + <that> + result clause.

source: It was a very long meeting. Everyone got frustrated.
correct: It was such a long meeting that everyone got frustrated.
explanation: <Such> + (a/an) + adjective + noun + <that> + result clause.

prompt: Rewrite using <Not only ... but also> with inversion
source: She is talented. She is also very hardworking.
correct: Not only is she talented, but she is also very hardworking.
Not only is she talented but also very hardworking.
explanation: <Not only> + inverted auxiliary + subject emphasizes both qualities.

source: My brother loves sports. I prefer reading.
correct: Whereas my brother loves sports, I prefer reading.
My brother loves sports, whereas I prefer reading.
explanation: <Whereas> introduces a direct contrast between two things/people.

source: Working from home saves commuting time. You miss social interaction at the office.
correct: Working from home saves commuting time. On the other hand, you miss social interaction at the office.
explanation: <On the other hand> introduces the opposite perspective.

source: It rained heavily all week. The river flooded.
correct: It rained heavily all week. As a result, the river flooded.
explanation: <As a result> introduces a consequence of the previous statement.

source: The flight was cancelled because of the storm.
correct: The flight was cancelled due to the storm.
Due to the storm, the flight was cancelled.
explanation: <Due to> + noun/gerund expresses cause (more formal than <because of>).

source: He didn't follow the instructions. He made several errors.
correct: He didn't follow the instructions. Consequently, he made several errors.
explanation: <Consequently> = formal <as a result>.

source: She left early because she wanted to catch the first train.
correct: She left early in order to catch the first train.
In order to catch the first train, she left early.
explanation: <In order to> + infinitive expresses purpose (more formal than just <to>).

source: He whispered because he didn't want to wake the baby.
correct: He whispered so as not to wake the baby.
hint: Negative purpose: <so as not to> + infinitive
explanation: <So as not to> + infinitive expresses a negative purpose.

source: The product is affordable. It also comes with a two-year warranty.
correct: The product is affordable. Furthermore, it comes with a two-year warranty.
explanation: <Furthermore> adds supporting information. More formal than <also>.

source: The apartment is spacious. It has a beautiful view too.
correct: The apartment is spacious. What's more, it has a beautiful view.
explanation: <What's more> adds an additional positive point. Semi-formal register.

source: He decided to walk. He didn't take a taxi.
correct: Rather than taking a taxi, he decided to walk.
He decided to walk rather than take a taxi.
explanation: <Rather than> + gerund/base verb expresses a preference or alternative.

source: He tried very hard, but he couldn't solve the puzzle.
correct: No matter how hard he tried, he couldn't solve the puzzle.
explanation: <No matter how> + adjective/adverb + clause expresses concession regardless of degree.

source: He knew it was wrong. He did it anyway.
correct: Even though he knew it was wrong, he did it anyway.
explanation: <Even though> = stronger version of <although>, emphasizes the contrast.

source: You can use my laptop if you return it by Friday.
correct: You can use my laptop provided that you return it by Friday.
You can use my laptop provided you return it by Friday.
explanation: <Provided (that)> = conditional connector meaning <only if>.

source: It doesn't matter if it rains. We'll go hiking.
correct: Whether it rains or not, we'll go hiking.
explanation: <Whether ... or not> expresses that the result is unchanged regardless.

source: She sings. She also plays the piano.
correct: As well as singing, she plays the piano.
She plays the piano as well as singing.
explanation: <As well as> + gerund adds an additional fact.

source: Everyone has arrived. Let's start the meeting.
correct: Seeing that everyone has arrived, let's start the meeting.
explanation: <Seeing that> = <given that>, introduces a reason.

prompt: Rewrite using <It is ... that> (cleft for emphasis)
source: The deadline caused all the stress.
correct: It is the deadline that caused all the stress.
It was the deadline that caused all the stress.
explanation: Cleft sentence: <It is/was> + focus + <that> + rest for emphasis.
